questions.stem: The disaccharide shown in the figure is:
options: Maltose
Lactose
Sucrose
Trehalose
questions.explanation: An α-D-glucopyranose (top) is linked through its C1 to C2 of a β-D-fructofuranose (five-membered ring, bottom): this is sucrose, α-D-glucopyranosyl (1→2) β-D-fructofuranoside. Trehalose is two glucopyranoses linked (1→1).

questions.stem: About the disaccharide shown in the figure:
options: It is an α-D-glucopyranosyl (1→2) β-D-fructofuranoside
It reduces Fehling's solution
Its hydrolysis products are levorotatory although the disaccharide itself is dextrorotatory
Its hydrolysis can be catalysed by β-D-fructosidase (invertase)
questions.explanation: Sucrose links both anomeric carbons (C1 of glucose, C2 of fructose), so it has no free aldehyde or keto group and is non-reducing. It is +66.5° while its hydrolysate is −28.2° (sucrose inversion), and invertase or α-D-glucosidase hydrolyses it.

questions.stem: About the disaccharide shown in the figure:
options: The left unit is a β-D-glucopyranose
Its two units are galactose and glucose joined by a β(1→4) glycosidic bond
It is a non-reducing disaccharide
It is found only in milk, at about 75 g/L in human milk
questions.explanation: This is β-lactose: β-D-galactopyranosyl (1→4) β-D-glucopyranose, so the left unit is galactose, not glucose. The glucose C1 stays free, which makes lactose reducing; it occurs in milk and nowhere else (≈75 g/L human, 48 g/L cow).

questions.stem: About the disaccharide shown in the figure:
options: It is trehalose
Its two glucose units are joined by an α(1→1) bond
It is a reducing disaccharide
Fungi and bacteria accumulate it in response to cold or desiccation
questions.explanation: Two α-D-glucopyranoses linked through both anomeric carbons (1→1) form trehalose. Because neither anomeric carbon is free it is non-reducing, like sucrose.

questions.stem: The two aldohexoses shown in the figure (Fischer projections) are:
options: Both of the D-series
C4 epimers
Diastereomers
Enantiomers
questions.explanation: Left is D-galactose, right is D-mannose: both have the C5 –OH on the right (D-series). They differ at two carbons (C2 and C4), so they are diastereomers, not epimers; they are not mirror images, so not enantiomers.

questions.stem: About the two aldohexoses shown in the figure:
options: The left one is the C4 epimer of D-glucose
The right one is the C2 epimer of D-glucose
Strong oxidation of the left one by nitric acid gives an optically inactive aldaric acid
Reduction of the right one gives D-sorbitol
questions.explanation: Left = D-galactose (C4 epimer of glucose), right = D-mannose (C2 epimer). Galactose + nitric acid gives mucic acid, inactive because of its plane of symmetry. Mannose is reduced to D-mannitol; D-sorbitol comes from glucose.

questions.stem: About the cyclic structure shown in the figure:
options: It is α-D-glucopyranose
It is β-D-glucopyranose
C1 is a hemiacetal carbon
The ring is closed between C1 and C4
questions.explanation: With the ring oxygen at the upper right, the C1 –OH pointing down defines the α anomer (up would be β). C1 is the anomeric (hemiacetal) carbon; a pyranose of an aldose closes C1–C5, not C1–C4 (that would be a furanose).

questions.stem: About the monosaccharide shown in the figure:
options: It is a ketohexose
Its ring is closed between C2 and C5
Its anomeric carbon is C1
Its solution turns polarized light to the right
questions.explanation: This is D-fructofuranose: a ketohexose whose five-membered ring forms between C2 and C5. Its anomeric (hemiketal) carbon is C2, and D-fructose is levorotatory (−92.2°).

questions.stem: About carbohydrates in general:
options: They are polyhydroxy-aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that produce them on hydrolysis
All of them satisfy the formula (CH₂O)n
Monosaccharides have the formula (CH₂O)n with n = 3 to 7
Monosaccharides can be hydrolysed into simpler carbohydrates
questions.explanation: Deoxyribose (C₅H₁₀O₄) does not fit (CH₂O)n, so carbohydrates are not always 'hydrates of carbon'. Monosaccharides are the simplest units and cannot be hydrolysed further.

questions.stem: About the biological roles of carbohydrates:
options: One gram of carbohydrate provides about 4 kcal
Glycogen is stored mainly in the liver and muscles
ABO blood group antigens are carbohydrate structures on the red blood cell surface
Cellulose is a linear polymer of α-D-glucose
questions.explanation: Cellulose is a linear polymer of β-D-glucose (β(1→4) bonds), which is why humans cannot digest it. The other three are stated in the lesson's list of roles.

questions.stem: About the classification of monosaccharides:
options: Glyceraldehyde is an aldotriose
Ribulose is an aldopentose
Sedoheptulose is a ketoheptose
Oligosaccharides contain more than 10 monosaccharide units
questions.explanation: Ribulose is the ketopentose (ribose is the aldopentose). Oligosaccharides contain 2–10 units; more than 10 makes a polysaccharide.

questions.stem: About asymmetric carbons (C*) of monosaccharides:
options: A carbon is asymmetric when it is attached to four different atoms or groups
Dihydroxyacetone has one asymmetric carbon
D-erythrose has 2 C* and therefore 4 stereoisomers
A linear aldohexose has 4 C* and therefore 16 stereoisomers
questions.explanation: The number of isomers is N = 2ⁿ (n = number of C*): 2² = 4 for erythrose, 2⁴ = 16 for aldohexoses (8 D + 8 L). Dihydroxyacetone is achiral — it has no asymmetric carbon.

questions.stem: About the D and L series:
options: The series is set by the –OH on the asymmetric carbon adjacent to the terminal primary alcohol
For glucose, this reference carbon is C4
Most sugars of higher animals, including man, are of the D configuration
D-glucose and L-glucose are C5 epimers
questions.explanation: For glucose the reference carbon is C5 (–OH right = D, left = L). D- and L-glucose are mirror images at every C*, so they are enantiomers, not epimers.

questions.stem: About Kiliani–Fischer synthesis and the D-aldose family:
options: It lengthens the chain of an aldose by one carbon at a time
There are 8 D-aldohexoses
Glucose, mannose and galactose are the most familiar D-aldohexoses
D-fructose is the only aldose that predominantly occurs in nature
questions.explanation: D-glucose is the aldose that predominates in nature; fructose is a ketose, not an aldose.

questions.stem: Which of the following are ketoses?
options: D-Xylulose
D-Erythrose
D-Ribose
D-Sedoheptulose
questions.explanation: D-Xylulose (5C) and D-sedoheptulose (7C) are among the physiologically important ketoses (with dihydroxyacetone, D-ribulose, D-fructose). Erythrose and ribose are aldoses.

questions.stem: About the cyclization of monosaccharides:
options: The pyranose ring of an aldose is formed between C1 and C5
The furanose ring of a ketose is formed between C1 and C4
The pyranose ring of a ketose is formed between C2 and C5
The chair form is the most stable conformation of glucose
questions.explanation: Aldoses: pyranose C1–C5, furanose C1–C4. Ketoses: pyranose C2–C6, furanose C2–C5. The chair form of glucose is more stable than the boat form.

questions.stem: Pure α-D-glucose is dissolved in water and its specific rotation is followed with a polarimeter:
options: The initial specific rotation is about +111°
The rotation falls until it stabilizes at about +52.5°
At equilibrium the solution contains only the β-form
This spontaneous change is called mutarotation
questions.explanation: α-D-glucose (+111°) and β-D-glucose (+19.2°) interconvert until an equilibrium mixture of both anomers at +52.5° is reached — not pure β.

questions.stem: About the measurement of optical activity:
options: It is measured with a polarimeter at 20 °C using the sodium D-line (589 nm)
In Biot's law, concentration is in g/mL and tube length in decimeters
A racemic mixture is dextrorotatory
Whether a sugar is (+) or (−) follows directly from its D or L configuration
questions.explanation: A racemic (equimolar D/L) mixture is optically inactive because the rotations cancel. The sign of rotation has no relationship with D/L configuration — D-fructose is levorotatory.

questions.stem: A solution contains D-glucose ([α] = +52°) and L-glucose at exactly the same concentration. Its observed rotation is:
questions.explanation: Enantiomers rotate light by equal amounts in opposite directions (L-glucose = −52°), and rotations are additive, so this racemic mixture shows no optical activity.

questions.stem: About the oxidation of monosaccharides:
options: Mild oxidation of an aldose gives an aldonic acid
Ketoses are oxidized under the same mild conditions
Oxidation of the terminal CH₂OH alone gives a uronic acid
Oxidation of both the aldehyde and the primary alcohol gives an aldaric acid
questions.explanation: Mild oxidation attacks only the aldehyde (aldonic acid) and ketoses do not react under these conditions. Strong oxidation of both ends → aldaric acid; of the CH₂OH only → uronic acid.

questions.stem: In the liver, bilirubin, hormones and drugs are made water-soluble for urinary or biliary elimination by conjugation with:
options: Gluconic acid
Glucuronic acid
Glucaric acid
Sorbitol
questions.explanation: Uronic acids (glucuronic acid) conjugate these substances into soluble glucuronides — hepatic detoxification. Gluconic acid is the aldonic acid and glucaric acid the aldaric acid of glucose.

questions.stem: A sugar solution heated with Fehling's solution in alkaline medium gives a red precipitate:
options: The precipitate is cuprous oxide
The sugar has been oxidized
Sucrose would give this result
The sugar is called a reducing sugar
questions.explanation: Cupric oxide oxidizes the aldose (to an aldonic acid) and is reduced to red cuprous oxide, so the sugar is 'reducing'. Sucrose has no free anomeric carbon and is non-reducing.

questions.stem: In poorly controlled diabetes, a sugar alcohol accumulates in the lens and nerves, contributing to cataract and neuropathy. About the reduction of monosaccharides:
options: Reduction of D-glucose gives D-sorbitol
Reduction of D-galactose gives D-dulcitol
Reduction of D-ribose gives D-mannitol
Mannitol raises intracranial pressure and is avoided in brain oedema
questions.explanation: Sorbitol and dulcitol cause osmotic swelling of cells when they accumulate. D-ribose gives D-ribitol, and mannitol is used to lower intracranial tension by forced diuresis.

questions.stem: About other chemical reactions of monosaccharides:
options: In dilute alkali, glucose, fructose and mannose interconvert through a common 1,2-enediol
Concentrated acid dehydrates pentoses into furfural
Dehydration of hexoses gives 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF)
ATP donates the phosphate in the formation of glucose 6-phosphate
questions.explanation: All four are taught: enolization (p43), dehydration losing three water molecules (p44), and esterification by phosphoric acid with ATP as donor (p45).

questions.stem: Methylation of the anomeric –OH of glucose:
options: Makes the sugar non-reducing
Makes the sugar more strongly reducing
Complete methylation helps locate glycosidic linkages in polysaccharides
Is the reaction that forms glucose 1-phosphate
questions.explanation: Blocking the anomeric –OH removes the reducing property. Complete methylation identifies which –OH groups are engaged in bonds (and protects them in synthesis); glucose 1-phosphate is a phosphate ester, not a methylation product.

questions.stem: About monosaccharide derivatives:
options: Deoxyribose carries a CH₂ group at carbon 2
Rhamnose is 6-deoxy-L-galactose
In amino sugars, the –OH at C2 is replaced by –NH₂
Sialic acid (NANA) is formed from pyruvic acid and D-glucosamine
questions.explanation: Fucose is 6-deoxy-L-galactose; rhamnose is 6-deoxy-L-mannose. Sialic acid (9C) comes from pyruvic acid (3C) + D-mannosamine (6C).

questions.stem: About vitamin C (ascorbic acid):
options: Only the L-form is biologically active
It is characterized by an ene-diol function
Humans synthesize it from glucose
Its deficiency causes scurvy through abnormal collagen synthesis
questions.explanation: Humans cannot synthesize ascorbic acid, which is why it is a water-soluble vitamin. Deficiency weakens collagen and vessel walls (scurvy).

questions.stem: Which of the following disaccharides are reducing?
options: Maltose
Cellobiose
Sucrose
Trehalose
questions.explanation: Maltose and cellobiose (both glucose (1→4) glucose) keep a free anomeric carbon. Sucrose (1→2) and trehalose (1→1) link both anomeric carbons and are non-reducing.

questions.stem: A patient with hepatic encephalopathy (raised plasma ammonia) is treated with lactulose:
options: Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide of galactose and fructose
Lactulose is absorbed in the small intestine
It converts NH₃ in the intestinal lumen into poorly absorbed NH₄⁺
Lactulose is made of two glucose units
questions.explanation: Lactulose (galactose + fructose) is neither digested nor absorbed; trapping ammonia as NH₄⁺ in the lumen lowers plasma NH₃.

questions.stem: About starch and glycogen:
options: Amylose is the water-insoluble, predominant component of starch
Glycogen has α(1→4) bonds with α(1→6) bonds at branch points
Glycogen contains a small protein, glycogenin, at its core
Glycogen is less branched than amylopectin
questions.explanation: Amylose is water-soluble and only 15–20% of starch; amylopectin (80–85%) is insoluble. Glycogen resembles amylopectin but with more branches; glycogenin initiates its synthesis.

questions.stem: About homopolysaccharides:
options: Chitin is made of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine units joined by β(1→4) bonds
Glucans are polymers of glucose and fructosans polymers of fructose
Humans digest cellulose using their amylases
Polysaccharides dissolve readily in water, forming true solutions
questions.explanation: Humans lack the enzyme that cleaves β-glycosidic bonds, so cellulose is indigestible fiber. Polysaccharides, with their high molecular weight, form colloidal solutions rather than dissolving readily.

questions.stem: About heterosides (glycosides):
options: In O-heterosides the aglycone is linked to the sugar through an oxygen atom
Nucleosides are N-heterosides
Sinigrin of black mustard seeds is an S-heteroside
Amygdalin can release hydrocyanic acid on enzymatic hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Heterosides are classed by the atom bonding sugar to aglycone: O (amygdalin, digitalin, rutin), N (purine/pyrimidine bases in nucleosides), S (sinigrin). Amygdalin is cyanogenic.

questions.stem: About glycoproteins and proteoglycans:
options: O-glycosidic linkages bind the carbohydrate to a serine or threonine –OH
N-glycosidic linkages bind the carbohydrate to the amide nitrogen of asparagine
In proteoglycans the carbohydrate part is less than 10%
Heparin is a secretory glycosaminoglycan
questions.explanation: Proteoglycans are dominated by their GAG chains (> 90% carbohydrate); it is glycoproteins whose carbohydrate content varies (1–90%).

questions.stem: About glycosaminoglycans (GAGs):
options: Hyaluronic acid is made of D-glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine
Chondroitin sulfate contains L-iduronic acid
Keratan sulfate keeps the cornea transparent
Hyaluronidase breaks α(1→4) linkages of hyaluronic acid around the ovum
questions.explanation: L-iduronic acid (C5 inversion of D-glucuronic acid) characterizes dermatan sulfate. Hyaluronidase cleaves the β(1→4) linkages, helping sperm penetration.

questions.stem: About monosaccharides of biological interest:
options: Normal glycemia is about 0.80 g/L
Fructose in seminal fluid is an energy substrate for spermatozoa
L-arabinose is fully metabolized by humans
Galactose is a constituent of lactose
questions.explanation: L-arabinose (and D-arabinose) are not metabolized by humans and are excreted in the urine without pathological consequences.
